take aback.verb type: action — dynamic, but a momentary event of surprising someone, so the progressive is odd: ✗ *her answer is taking me aback*. It has no linking or stative use.
take aback.passive: **yes**, and the passive is the usual form — *I was taken aback by how blunt her answer was*; *she looked taken aback*. The active *her answer took me aback* is the marked one.

take after.verb type: **stative** — a resemblance, like *resemble* itself, not anything the subject does. It rejects the progressive: ✗ *she is taking after her mother*.
take after.passive: **no** — a stative resemblance verb, and the prepositional object cannot be promoted: ✗ *her mother is taken after by her*, ✗ *his grandfather was taken after*.

take apart.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: dismantling (*he's taking the carburetor apart*), defeating an opponent, and pulling an argument to pieces.
take apart.passive: **yes** in every sense — *the carburetor was taken apart on the kitchen table*; *we were taken apart, 42 to 3*; *the whole third chapter was taken apart*.

take aside.verb type: action — dynamic: a single act of leading someone away for a private word. Progressive is fine — *he's taking her aside now*.
take aside.passive: **yes** — *I was taken aside after practice*; *the two students who had been whispering were taken aside*.

take away.verb type: action — dynamic in the remove sense (*they're taking his license away*). The arithmetic sense is a frozen classroom formula that does not inflect — *six take away two is four*, ✗ *six is taking away two* — and *take away from* (lessen) is closer to **stative**.
take away.passive: **restricted** — full passive in the remove sense: *his license was taken away for six months*, *our plates were taken away*. None in the other senses: ✗ *two is taken away from six*, ✗ *the food is taken away from by the loud music*.

take back.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: retracting, returning a purchase, readmitting a person, and (of a song or a smell) sending someone back in memory.
take back.passive: **restricted** — senses 1–3 passivize freely: *the sweater was taken back*, *not one word of it was taken back*, *she was taken back two years later*. The memory sense resists it: ✗ *I am taken back to high school by that song*.

take down.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: writing down, dismantling, defeating or arresting, and the idiomatic *take down a peg*.
take down.passive: **yes** — *my name and address were taken down*; *the tent was taken down in the rain*; *he was taken down in the parking lot*; *he needs to be taken down a peg*.

take for.verb type: **stative** — a judgment or a mistaken belief about identity, not an act, so the progressive is out: ✗ *I am taking him for a security guard*. The fixed *take for granted* is the same.
take for.passive: **yes**, unusually for a stative verb — *he was taken for a security guard because of the jacket*; *it was taken for granted that the room would be free*; *she doesn't want to be taken for granted*.

take in.verb type: action — dynamic in all five senses: absorbing information (*she sat taking it all in*), sheltering, deceiving, narrowing a garment, and going to see a show.
take in.passive: **yes** — *two foster kids were taken in last spring*; *the waist was taken in two inches*. The deceive sense lives mostly in the passive: *don't be taken in by the discount*.

take off.verb type: action — dynamic everywhere: removing something worn, leaving the ground, bolting, suddenly succeeding, and deducting time or money.
take off.passive: **restricted** — the transitive senses passivize: *shoes must be taken off at the door*, *ten dollars was taken off the bill*. The intransitive senses have no passive at all: ✗ *it was taken off by the plane*, ✗ *the business was taken off*.

take on.verb type: action — dynamic in the accept-work, hire, and fight senses. Sense 3 (*his voice took on an edge*) is an inchoative change of state — still dynamic, but with an inanimate, non-agentive subject.
take on.passive: **restricted** — the agentive senses passivize: *three new clients were taken on*, *he was taken on as an apprentice*, *the state was taken on and beaten*. Sense 3 does not: ✗ *an edge was taken on by his voice*.

take out.verb type: action — dynamic in all four verbal senses: removing, escorting someone out, obtaining something official, and destroying a target. (*Takeout*, the food, is a noun.)
take out.passive: **yes** in every sense — *the trash was taken out before dinner*; *I was taken out for my birthday*; *a loan was taken out against the house*; *the bridge was taken out by one missile*.

take out on.verb type: action — dynamic: an act of venting, and progressive is normal — *you're taking it out on the kids again*.
take out on.passive: **restricted** — the feeling can be promoted: *his frustration was taken out on whoever was closest*. The person after *on* cannot: ✗ *the kids were taken it out on*, ✗ *I was taken out on*.

take over.verb type: action — dynamic: assuming a duty, seizing a company or a place, or (of panic, vines, a habit) becoming dominant.
take over.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the class was taken over when the teacher quit*; *we were taken over by a bigger firm*; *the airport was taken over before dawn*. The intransitive *take over for someone* has no passive.

take to.verb type: action — inceptive rather than fully dynamic: it names the moment liking or a habit begins, which is why the progressive is odd (✗ *she is taking to the new nanny*) while *has taken to getting up at five* is normal. Sense 3, heading for a place, is plainly dynamic.
take to.passive: **no** — the prepositional object stays put in all three senses: ✗ *the new nanny was taken to right away*, ✗ *running was taken to after the surgery*, ✗ *the streets were taken to that night*.

take up.verb type: action — dynamic in the start-a-hobby, resume, raise-a-matter, and tailoring senses. The occupy-space sense is closer to **stative**: *that couch takes up half the room* describes a state, not an event.
take up.passive: **yes** — *half the room is taken up by that couch*; *the hem was taken up an inch*; *the story was taken up again after the interruption*; *it should be taken up with HR*.

take up on.verb type: action — dynamic: a single act of accepting an offer. Progressive is fine — *I'm taking you up on that*.
take up on.passive: **restricted** — the person passivizes naturally: *she was taken up on her offer of a ride*; *nobody was ever taken up on that invitation*. The offer after *on* cannot move: ✗ *the offer was taken her up on*.

take up with.verb type: action — dynamic and inceptive: beginning to keep company with someone. Progressive is possible but rare — *she's been taking up with the wrong people*.
take up with.passive: **no** — the object of *with* resists promotion: ✗ *a rough crowd was taken up with by him*, ✗ *he was taken up with after the divorce*.

tear apart.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: ripping to pieces, dividing or distressing people, and ransacking a place.
tear apart.passive: **yes** — *the cushion was torn apart by the dog*; *the town was torn apart by the scandal*; *the apartment was torn apart looking for the passport*.

tear at.verb type: action — dynamic, and durative in both senses: repeated pulling (*she was tearing at the knot*) and guilt that keeps working on someone (*it tears at me*).
tear at.passive: **restricted**, and marginal at best — a prepositional passive is barely possible for the physical sense: ?*the wrapping had been torn at*. The distress sense has none: ✗ *he was torn at by guilt for years*.

tear away.verb type: action — dynamic: forcing someone (usually yourself) to leave something absorbing, or ripping something off by force.
tear away.passive: **restricted** — fine when someone else does it: *the kids were torn away from the screen*; *the plastic film was torn away*. The reflexive use, which is the common one, has no passive: ✗ *myself was torn away from the game*.

tear down.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: demolishing, belittling a person, and striking a stage or rig.
tear down.passive: **yes** — *the old high school was torn down in June*; *the stage was torn down in under two hours*; *nobody likes being torn down in public*.

tear into.verb type: action — dynamic: a sudden burst of energy aimed at a person, a plate of food, or a job. Progressive is normal — *he's tearing into the sandwich*.
tear into.passive: **restricted** — the prepositional passive is awkward even in the criticize sense: ?*he was torn into in front of the whole staff*. The energy sense refuses it: ✗ *the presents were torn into by the kids*.

tear off.verb type: action — dynamic: ripping something free, pulling clothing off fast, or (intransitively) leaving at speed.
tear off.passive: **restricted** — the transitive senses passivize: *the stub was torn off and mailed in*; *his wet jacket was torn off*. The leave-fast sense is intransitive and has none: ✗ *the driveway was torn off down*.

tear out.verb type: action — dynamic: ripping something out of what held it, stripping a surface, or (intransitively) leaving very fast.
tear out.passive: **restricted** — the transitive senses passivize: *three pages had been torn out of the manual*; *the carpet was torn out and hardwood was found underneath*. The leave-fast sense has no object and no passive.

tear through.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: moving through something violently (*the fire tore through four buildings*) and getting through it fast (*she tore through her savings*).
tear through.passive: **no** — the prepositional object cannot be promoted in either sense: ✗ *four buildings were torn through by the fire*, ✗ *two pizzas were torn through in ten minutes*.

tear up.verb type: action — dynamic: ripping paper, canceling an agreement, chewing up a surface. Sense 4 is a different, regular verb (*teared up*, from the noun *tear* /tɪr/) and is an intransitive change of state.
tear up.passive: **restricted** — the three transitive senses passivize: *the letter was torn up without being read*; *the contract was torn up in March*; *the lawn was torn up by the plows*. The eyes sense cannot: ✗ *he was teared up*.

tell apart.verb type: **stative** — an ability to perceive a difference, not an act, which is why it lives under *can* and the negative and rejects the progressive: ✗ *I am telling the twins apart*.
tell apart.passive: **yes**, though almost always under a modal — *the twins can't be told apart over the phone*; *the copies are so good that they can't be told apart by experts*.

tell off.verb type: action — dynamic: a single act of scolding someone to their face. Progressive is fine — *she was telling him off in front of everybody*.
tell off.passive: **yes**, and the informal *get*-passive is very common — *he got told off for showing up late again*; *I was told off in front of the whole staff*.

tell on.verb type: action — dynamic in the informing sense (*he's telling on me again*). The show-an-effect sense is gradual and closer to **stative**: *the late nights are starting to tell on her*.
tell on.passive: **restricted** — the informal *get*-passive is heard in the schoolyard sense: *I got told on*; the *be*-passive is stiffer: ?*he was told on by his sister*. The show-an-effect sense has none: ✗ *his knees were told on by twenty years of construction work*.

think back.verb type: action — dynamic: a deliberate mental act, and the progressive is normal — *thinking back, I should have said no*.
think back.passive: **no** — there is no direct object at all, and what is remembered sits behind *to* or *on* and cannot be promoted: ✗ *that summer was thought back on*, ✗ *1998 was thought back to*.

think of.verb type: **stative** in the opinion sense — a held attitude, not an act: ✗ *he is thinking highly of your work*. Dynamic in the come-up-with, recall, and consider senses: *we're thinking of moving in the spring*.
think of.passive: **restricted** — the opinion sense passivizes in fixed formulas: *she is very highly thought of*, *the new policy isn't much thought of*. The other senses barely do: ?*who was that idea thought of by*, ✗ *her last name couldn't be thought of*.

think out.verb type: action — dynamic: working a plan through to its details in advance. Progressive is possible but uncommon — *he's still thinking it out*.
think out.passive: **yes**, and the participle is where you usually meet it — *the plan wasn't thought out at all*; *it was a beautifully thought-out answer*.

think over.verb type: action — dynamic and durative: deliberating before deciding. Progressive is fine — *I'm still thinking it over*.
think over.passive: **yes**, though the active is far more common — *the offer was thought over for a week before she answered*; *it deserves to be thought over carefully*.

think through.verb type: action — dynamic: following an idea out to its consequences. Progressive is fine — *we're thinking through what happens if the funding falls apart*.
think through.passive: **yes** — *this hasn't been thought through*; *the cost of maintaining it was never thought through*.

think up.verb type: **action** — dynamic throughout: a single act of invention, fine in the progressive (*he's still thinking up excuses*).
think up.passive: **yes**, though the active is far more common — *the whole scheme was thought up in an afternoon*, *that name was thought up on the way to the show*.

throw away.verb type: **action** — dynamic in all three senses: discarding, squandering a lead, and tossing off a line are all things done.
throw away.passive: **yes** — *the box was thrown away*, *a two-goal lead was thrown away in ten minutes*. The participle also hardens into the adjective *a throwaway remark*.

throw back.verb type: **action** — dynamic in every sense, from returning a fish to delaying a schedule.
throw back.passive: **yes** — *the fish was thrown back*, *the attack was thrown back at the ridge*. Sense 4 exists **only** as a passive: *we were thrown back on paper files*, never ✗ *the outage threw us back on paper files* in that fixed shape.

throw in.verb type: **action** — dynamic: adding a freebie or dropping a remark into a conversation.
throw in.passive: **restricted** — natural in the freebie and remark senses (*free shipping was thrown in*, *a comment about the budget was thrown in*), but the idioms refuse: ✗ *the towel was thrown in*, and *throw in with* has no passive at all.

throw off.verb type: **action** — dynamic in all four senses; even the *emit* sense (*the radiator throws off heat*) reports ongoing activity, not a state.
throw off.passive: **yes** — *I was thrown off by the change in schedule*, *the dogs were thrown off at the creek*, *a lot of heat is thrown off by that old radiator*.

throw on.verb type: **action** — dynamic, and the hurry is part of the meaning: clothes, music, or coffee put on fast.
throw on.passive: **restricted** — the agentless passive is fine (*a jacket was thrown on over pajamas*), but naming the agent sounds wrong: ✗ *a sweater was thrown on by her*.

throw out.verb type: **action** — dynamic in all five senses: discarding, ejecting, rejecting, floating an idea, wrenching your back.
throw out.passive: **yes** in senses 1–4 — *the leftovers were thrown out*, *he was thrown out after the second warning*, *the case was thrown out by the judge*. Sense 5 resists an agent: ✗ *his back was thrown out by him*, though *my back got thrown out* is idiomatic.

throw over.verb type: **action** — dynamic, and dated: abandoning a partner or an ally, mostly a novelist's verb now.
throw over.passive: **yes**, and the passive is the commoner shape — *he was thrown over the week before the wedding*.

throw together.verb type: **action** — dynamic; sense 2 (chance acquaintance) is close to a change of state but still reports an event.
throw together.passive: **yes** — *a presentation was thrown together in twenty minutes*, and sense 2 is effectively passive-only: *the two of them were thrown together on a project*. The participle is adjectival too: *it looks thrown together*.

throw up.verb type: **action** — dynamic everywhere: vomiting, building fast, turning up a result.
throw up.passive: **restricted** — yes in the transitive senses (*forty houses were thrown up in a year*, *three names we hadn't seen were thrown up by the search*); no in the vomit sense, which has no object, and none for the idiom: ✗ *his hands were thrown up*.

thrust upon.verb type: **action** — dynamic, and formal: forcing a role or a duty on someone who did not ask for it.
thrust upon.passive: **yes**, and the passive is the normal form — *the role was thrust upon her when the director resigned*, *some have greatness thrust upon them*.

tread on.verb type: **action** — dynamic in both senses; the literal one is British-leaning, since an American says *step on*.
tread on.passive: **restricted** — the prepositional passive works best in the idiom (*nobody likes having their toes trodden on*); the literal *my foot was trodden on* is grammatical but bookish in American English, where *somebody stepped on my foot* is the live sentence.

wake up.verb type: **action** — dynamic; senses 1 and 3 are inchoative (entering wakefulness or awareness), sense 2 is causative — you make someone else do it.
wake up.passive: **restricted** — only the causative sense passivizes: *I was woken up by the delivery truck*, *the whole floor was woken up*. The intransitive senses have no object and so no passive: ✗ *it was woken up at four*.

wake up to.verb type: **action** — dynamic and inchoative: the moment awareness arrives, not the state of knowing. The progressive is fine: *the industry is only now waking up to the problem*.
wake up to.passive: **no** — the prepositional passive is unavailable here: ✗ *the problem is being woken up to by the industry*, ✗ *six inches of snow was woken up to*.

wear away.verb type: **action** — dynamic and gradual; the intransitive use is the inchoative twin of the transitive (*the lettering wore away* ≈ something wore it away).
wear away.passive: **yes** in the transitive sense — *the stone had been worn away by centuries of water*, *the lettering has been worn away*. The intransitive use has no object and so no passive: ✗ *the path was worn away to bare dirt by itself*.

wear down.verb type: **action** — dynamic in both senses, and gradual by definition; the participle also works as an adjective after *be*: *the heels are worn down on one side*.
wear down.passive: **yes** — *the letters were worn down to blanks by years of typing*, *I was worn down until I said yes*. No passive of the intransitive *the treads wore down*.

wear in.verb type: **action** — dynamic, and British; the American equivalent is *break in*. The intransitive use (*the boots will wear in*) is the same event told from the object's side.
wear in.passive: **yes** in the transitive sense — *the shoes were worn in around the house first*, *a stiff glove needs to be worn in*. None for the intransitive.

wear off.verb type: **action** — dynamic, gradual, and intransitive: an effect fading, not a state. The progressive is natural: *the anesthetic is wearing off*.
wear off.passive: **no** — there is no object to promote: ✗ *the novelty was worn off*, ✗ *the caffeine had been worn off by noon*.

wear on.verb type: **action** — dynamic in both senses: time dragging past (*as the evening wore on*) and something grinding at a person's patience.
wear on.passive: **no** — sense 1 is objectless, and the prepositional object of sense 2 will not promote: ✗ *I am worn on by his voice*, ✗ *she was being worn on by the commute*. Use *wear down* when you need the passive.

wear out.verb type: **action** — dynamic; the participle is fully adjectival after *be*, which is where learners meet it first: *the brake pads are worn out*.
wear out.passive: **yes** — *those sneakers were worn out in one season*, *the kids were worn out by two hours at the playground*. The idiom resists: ✗ *their welcome was worn out*.

weave in.verb type: **action** — dynamic, literal with thread and figurative with a theme or a reference.
weave in.passive: **yes** — *a reference to the earlier data was woven in*, *the folk tune was woven in under the strings*. Note the participle is *woven*, not *weaved*, in this sense.

win back.verb type: **action** — dynamic: regaining trust, customers, or a title you had lost.
win back.passive: **yes** — *the seat was won back in the fall*, *the title she lost in 2019 was won back last spring*. With a person it is possible but less common: *she was won back eventually*.

win out.verb type: **action** — dynamic and intransitive; what it beats goes after *over*, not into an object slot: *won out over the prettier design*.
win out.passive: **no** — no object anywhere, so nothing can be promoted: ✗ *the end was won out in*, ✗ *the prettier one was won out over*.

win over.verb type: **action** — dynamic: bringing a doubter around, usually over time.
win over.passive: **yes**, and it is common — *the whole committee was won over in ten minutes*, *even the critics were won over by the second half*.

win through.verb type: **action** — dynamic and intransitive; British, where an American says *pull through* or *win out*.
win through.passive: **no** — objectless, so there is nothing to passivize: ✗ *the final was won through to*.

wind down.verb type: **action** — dynamic in both senses; sense 1 (a person or a party relaxing) is intransitive, sense 2 (closing an operation down) is causative.
wind down.passive: **restricted** — the causative sense passivizes readily (*the program is being wound down over two years*, *the European operations were wound down in 2019*); the relaxing sense has no object: ✗ *an hour was wound down after the shift*.

wind up.verb type: **action** — dynamic; sense 1 (*wind up in court*) is intransitive and close to *end up*, and sense 4 lives mostly in the adjectival participle after *be*: *the kids are all wound up*.
wind up.passive: **restricted** — yes in the transitive senses (*the meeting was wound up early*, *the old clock was wound up every Sunday*, *the kids were wound up by all that sugar*); no in sense 1: ✗ *a diner was wound up at*.

withdraw into.verb type: **action** — dynamic and inchoative: entering a retreat from other people, not occupying one. *He was withdrawing into himself* is fine.
withdraw into.passive: **no** — the object after *into* is reflexive or abstract and will not promote: ✗ *himself was withdrawn into*, ✗ *a silence was withdrawn into by her*.

write back.verb type: **action** — dynamic: sending a reply, with or without naming the person replied to.
write back.passive: **no** — the person sits inside the phrase but resists promotion: ✗ *I was written back*, ✗ *her cousin was written back the same night*. Say *she got a reply* instead.

write down.verb type: **action** — dynamic in both the everyday sense and the accounting sense.
write down.passive: **yes** — *the address was written down on the back of a receipt*, *the loan was written down by forty percent*.

write in.verb type: **action** — dynamic; sense 1 (inserting a name or a clause) is transitive, sense 2 (writing to a paper or a station) intransitive.
write in.passive: **restricted** — yes for sense 1: *her name was written in on hundreds of ballots*, *the clause was written in by hand*. Sense 2 has no object: ✗ *the paper was written in to by listeners*.

write off.verb type: **action** — dynamic in all three senses: canceling a debt, giving up on someone, and (British) wrecking a car.
write off.passive: **yes** — *the balance was written off*, *he was written off too early*, *the album was written off when it came out*.

write out.verb type: **action** — dynamic: setting something down in full, producing a document, or removing a character or an heir.
write out.passive: **yes** — *a prescription was written out*, *the number should be written out in words*, *she was written out of the show after season three*.

write up.verb type: **action** — dynamic in all three senses: turning notes into an account, filing a disciplinary report, and revaluing an asset upward.
write up.passive: **yes** — *the results were written up over the weekend*, *he was written up for being late three times*, *the asset was written up after the appraisal*.
